turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): oh, sorry we're late. the tram was an absolute mess, and then I couldn't find the right entrance.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): you're right, come in and sit down. we've still got you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): he was gunna cancel. I told him I'd march him here if he did.
[SEG0004] person_4 (NURSE): doctor, want his numbers? I did them out the front.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): please.
[SEG0006] person_4 (NURSE): blood pressure was 128 over 78, pulse 88, temp 37.4, sats 98 percent. he said no to the scales.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): ta. so what's actually brought you in?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): um. my eyes have gone yellow. and I'm wrecked, like no energy, and my pee's gone really dark.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): right. when did the yellow start?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): uh I don't know, doctor. I can't put a date on it. sometime after we got home.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I saw it about ten days ago. sunday arvo, he was crashed on the couch and the whites were yellow.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): so we'll call it roughly ten days, though you're not sure of the day. was the dark pee the same stretch?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): yeah, dark like tea. I don't know if it came before the eyes or after. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): and the tiredness, is that every day?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): pretty much. I get home and I'm done. even the walk to the tram's an effort.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): he's been sleeping through his lunch break. that's not like him.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): any vomiting? any fever? pain in the belly?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): no vomiting. no fever. tummy's a bit sore up on the right, not agony.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): and the poo, has it gone pale? any itching?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): poo's a bit pale, yeah. itching, no.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): the food thing. where did you eat, and where were you?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): err, vietnam, a couple of weeks. roadside stalls, plastic stools, noodles and meat on sticks. I don't know, doctor, half of it I couldn't name.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): three others from the trip are crook as well. one girl's gone yellow, her mum texted.

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): let me play that back. yellow eyes for about ten days, tea-coloured urine, exhausted, a bit of pain under the right ribs, pale stools, street food in vietnam, and others in the group unwell. no vomit, no fever, no itch. fair?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): yeah. I think so. it all blurs a bit, I don't know.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): any medicines, things you take now or something you've stopped?

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I was taking neurofen, the 400 milligram ones, twice a day for a headache on the trip. stopped it when we got back, my gut went funny. and they wrote me a script for an antibiotic over there, but I never filled it, didn't take one.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): yeah I binned the packet. he hasn't had any since the flight.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): no. none.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): family. any diabetes, blood pressure, liver problems?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): um my father had diabetes in his fifties, mum did not, my other sister's got pressure but no sugar. livers, I don't know, doctor. nobody's mentioned it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): and day to day. work, hours, what you eat, exercise, grog?

[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I drive a forklift at a warehouse in Footscray, early starts, six till two. diet's pretty rubbish, pies and servo food mostly. I don't exercise. and I don't drink, never have.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. the whites of your eyes are yellow. tummy's soft, tender just under the right ribs, and there's no rash on the chest or arms.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely a hepatitis, possibly hepatitis A from the street food, but that's a working idea, not confirmed. the neurofen is less likely, given the others are sick, though I won't fully rule it out.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book liver blood tests and hepatitis serology for today. if those come back abnormal we might do an ultrasound of the liver, not before. stay off the neurofen, rest and fluids, and I'll see you early next week with the results. if you start vomiting and can't keep water down, or you get confused or drowsy, come straight in, don't wait.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): ok. early next week then. I don't know, doctor, I just want it gone.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): one step at a time. pathology's on the way out, reception will point you.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Patient declined to be weighed / said no to the scales.
Dark urine described as 'dark like tea'.
Fatigue detail: even the walk to the tram is an effort, and caregiver reports he has been sleeping through his lunch break.
Recent travel/exposure history missing: returned from Vietnam after a couple of weeks, ate roadside/street-stall food (noodles and meat on sticks).
Exposure history missing: three others from the trip are also unwell, and one has developed jaundice.
Medication history incomplete: patient stopped Nurofen when they got back because his 'gut went funny'.
Medication history missing: an antibiotic was prescribed overseas but the prescription was never filled and he did not take any antibiotic; caregiver added he has had none since the flight.
Allergies detail should specify no allergies to medicines or foods, not just generic 'allergies absent'.
Family history detail missing: no known family liver problems; mother did not have diabetes.
